title: Connecting agents to Doctolib and your practice management software
metaDescription: Doctolib scheduling for health centers: connect agents to Doctolib and your practice management software with no double entry and no overhaul. The step-by-step method, with control kept.
contentHtml:
Connecting agents to Doctolib and to a center’s practice management software does not require overhauling the information system. It takes three rules: read-only by default, write access on an explicit scope, and traceability of every action. That is the short answer for managers searching for “Doctolib scheduling for health centers”: how to keep calendars accurate without the front desk copying the same information into two tools. The rollout then happens in stages. Each stage is a decision by the center’s management, not an IT decision.

This article is for the management of a health center or medical center. It describes what an agent can do between the online calendar and the practice management software, how to eliminate double entry, who stays in control of write actions, and where to start without taking risks.

Key takeaways
  • An agent works in your existing tools, with defined permissions: no software change and no custom interface project to get started.
  • The first step is always read-only: the agent observes Doctolib and the practice management software, flags discrepancies, writes nothing.
  • Write access then opens case by case, first with human validation of each action, then autonomously once reliability has been demonstrated.
  • Every action is logged, assigned to a human supervisor and reversible. The center remains the data controller under the GDPR.
  • An action you can take today: write down, for each piece of data (patient, appointment, absence, procedure), which tool is the source of truth.

Do you need a heavy IT project to connect agents to Doctolib?

No, not to get started. The image of a months-long integration project comes from custom interface projects and software changes. An agent replaces neither Doctolib nor the practice management software: it works inside them, as a team member would with their own access.

The difference from older approaches lies in how the work is done. Fixed-script robots replayed a sequence of clicks and broke at the slightest screen change. An agent reads what is in front of it and adapts to the context. The difference is explained in detail in our article on agentic AI versus classic robotic automation in healthcare.

What determines success, then, is not the technology. It is governance: who authorizes the agent to read, who authorizes it to write, on what scope, and who checks. A center that has answered these questions before connecting anything moves fast. A center that discovers them along the way stalls.

One precaution remains necessary. What an agent can do depends on the access your software vendors allow. Before starting, reread the terms of your Doctolib contract and of your practice management software, and ask your contacts at each of them.

What can an agent do on a health center’s Doctolib calendar?

An agent keeps the online calendar consistent with what the center’s back office knows: practitioners’ absences, open slots, appointments to reschedule, incomplete patient records. These are repetitive tasks, done by hand today by the front desk, often at the end of the day.

In practice, in a multidisciplinary center, the Doctolib calendar changes constantly. A doctor leaves for training, a physical therapist changes their days on site, a dentist adds a half-day. The information already exists somewhere, in the internal schedule or with management. The work consists of carrying it over everywhere, without missing anything.

TaskWhat the agent readsWhat it proposes or writes
Practitioner absenceThe center’s internal scheduleClosing the affected slots in Doctolib
Appointments to rescheduleAppointments booked on a closed slotThe list of patients to call back, for the front desk
Incomplete patient recordThe Doctolib appointment and the record in the practice management softwareA flag before the consultation
Slot opened by mistakeThe bookable slots of an absent practitionerAn alert, then the correction after validation

The last link also matters for billing. An attended appointment becomes a procedure, then an invoice, then often a third-party payment (tiers payant: the patient pays nothing upfront, insurers pay the provider directly) share to collect from mandatory insurance (AMO) and supplementary insurance (AMC). An accurate calendar upstream means fewer discrepancies to correct downstream.

How do you avoid double entry between Doctolib and the practice management software?

The safest method is to designate, for each piece of data, a single tool as the source of truth, then hand the copying to the other tools over to the agent. Double entry rarely comes from a missing tool. It comes from data with no clear owner.

In many centers, a patient’s identity is entered when the appointment is booked online, then re-entered in the practice management software at reception. The two versions diverge: an address, a spelling, a date of birth. Syncing the Doctolib calendar with the practice management software therefore starts with a decision, not with a connector.

DataSource of truth (example)What the agent does
Appointments and slotsDoctolibReads appointments, flags those without a record
Patient identity and recordPractice management softwareCompares and flags discrepancies, corrects nothing on its own at first
Practitioners’ absences and presenceThe center’s internal scheduleCarries them over to Doctolib
Procedures and billingPractice management softwareReads to match attended appointments with billed procedures

This table is an example. Your center can make other choices, for example making the schedule kept in the practice management software the source of truth. What matters is that there is only one answer per row, known to the whole team.

The right reflex: write this table on one page before connecting anything and have the front desk validate it. They are the ones who know where discrepancies arise.

Why start in read-only mode?

Read-only mode lets you check that the agent understands your workflows before it changes anything. During this phase, it logs in, observes Doctolib and the practice management software, and produces findings. It writes nothing.

This phase serves three goals. First, validating its understanding of the workflows: can the agent tell an absence from a slot blocked for a team meeting? Next, calibrating: adjusting its rules to the center’s actual habits, which always differ a little from the written procedures. Finally, building the team’s trust, with no risk at all to patients or calendars.

The typical deliverable is a daily list of discrepancies: appointments without a record, slots open for an absent practitioner, identities that do not match between the two tools. The front desk checks each line. When the list is accurate, day after day, the question of write access can be raised.

This list often has value in itself. It shows management where the real discrepancies are, something no dashboard usually shows.

How do you open write access without losing control?

You open write access on a specific case, with human validation of each action, then move to autonomy only once reliability has been demonstrated on that case. The scope is written down in black and white: which action, in which tool, for which practitioners or which sites.

  1. Choose a narrow case. For example: closing in Doctolib the slots of a practitioner whose absence is entered in the internal schedule.
  2. Have it propose, not write. The agent prepares the change, a team member accepts or rejects it.
  3. Track rejections. Each rejected proposal is analyzed: a misunderstood rule, a special case, wrong source data.
  4. Move to autonomy on this case only. When the proposals are consistently accurate, management authorizes the agent to write on its own, with after-the-fact review.
  5. Open the next case. And start again at step 2.

This progression costs time at first: the team validates actions it could have done itself. That is intentional. It is during this phase that the team learns what the agent does and agrees to hand over the next steps.

The trap: opening write access on “the whole calendar” at once. A single poorly calibrated rule can then affect dozens of appointments before anyone notices.

Who stays in control of write actions?

Management and the operational team stay in control: every action by the agent is logged, assigned to a human supervisor and reversible. No write is final without a trace. If a change causes a problem, you know who authorized it and when, and you can roll it back.

This rule is not just a matter of convenience. A center’s appointments and records contain health data. The center is the data controller, and the provider that supplies the agents acts as a processor. Chapter IV of the GDPR then requires a contract between the two (Article 28), under which the processor processes data only on the controller’s documented instructions. The same chapter requires security measures appropriate to the risk (Article 32) and, for processing likely to result in a high risk, an impact assessment (Article 35).

The processing must also appear in the center’s record of processing activities, which the CNIL (the French data protection authority) presents as the tool for listing and managing compliance. In practice, add an entry for the activity handed to the agents: purpose, data involved, retention periods, processor.

For the content of the log itself (which actions to record, for how long, who has access), see what an AI agent should log in a healthcare environment. The broader framework is covered in what the regulatory framework really requires of AI in healthcare.

Where do you start a rollout?

A rollout starts with a read-only connection, data exploration and calibration, then the activation of the first agents in supervised mode, with the operational team validating each action. Expansion comes next, stage by stage.

Here is the sequence, seen from management’s side:

  1. Read-only connection. The agent receives view-only access to Doctolib and to the practice management software.
  2. Exploration and calibration. It observes the actual workflows, the team corrects its understanding, the discrepancy list becomes reliable.
  3. First supervised agents. Write access opens on a narrow case, each action is validated by a person.
  4. Expansion in stages. New cases, wider scope, move to autonomy: each stage is the subject of a management decision.

This progression avoids the tunnel effect of traditional IT projects, where you discover the result at the end. At each stage, the center sees what the agent brings and decides whether or not to move forward. That is how Granit’s agents work: they start by observing, then write under your team’s control, and every action stays traced and reversible.

For a group of several centers, start with a pilot site and a willing team. The rules calibrated on that site then carry over to the others, taking differences in organization into account. Managing several sites is covered in our article on multi-site groups.

How do you decide to move to the next stage?

You move to the next stage when the current stage has been measured and judged reliable by the team that supervises it. The decision belongs to the operational side. IT says whether it is possible, management says whether it is desirable.

A few simple metrics are enough, tracked at the pilot center:

  • the number of discrepancies detected each day between Doctolib and the practice management software, and how it changes;
  • the share of the agent’s proposals accepted without correction by the team;
  • the time the front desk still spends on copying and calendar checks;
  • incidents: changes canceled, patients poorly informed, slots closed by mistake.

Measure these points before starting, even roughly, to have a baseline. Without a starting point, it is impossible to say whether a stage has brought anything. Other back-office metrics useful to management are presented in the healthcare back-office KPIs to track.

A stage may also not be cleared. If a case remains too variable, for example absences entered irregularly in the internal schedule, it is better to fix the source data first than to widen the agent’s scope. The agent often reveals an organizational problem no one saw. Addressing it is part of the benefit.

faqItems.question: Can Doctolib calendar management be automated?
faqItems.answer: Yes, part of calendar management can be handed to agents that work in Doctolib and in the center’s practice management software. For example, they carry over practitioners’ absences and flag appointments to reschedule or incomplete records. What is possible depends on the access your software vendors allow, which you should check in your contracts before starting.

faqItems.question: How do you avoid double entry between Doctolib and the practice management software?
faqItems.answer: For each piece of data, designate a single tool as the source of truth: for example, Doctolib for appointments and the practice management software for patient identity and billing. Copying to the other tools is then handed to the agent, instead of being re-entered by the front desk. This decision is made before connecting anything.

faqItems.question: Who stays in control of write actions?
faqItems.answer: The center’s management and operational team stay in control. Every action by the agent is logged, assigned to a human supervisor and reversible. The center remains the data controller under the GDPR and the provider acts as a processor, on documented instructions.

faqItems.question: Where do you start a rollout?
faqItems.answer: A rollout starts with a read-only connection: the agent observes Doctolib and the practice management software and flags discrepancies without changing anything. Calibration comes next, then write access is opened on a narrow case with human validation of each action. Expansion happens in stages, each one decided by management.
